baby-toddler-fruit-and-vegetables-with-g.title: Baby Toddler fruit and vegetables, with grain

content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler fruit and vegetables, with grain is a ready‑to‑serve baby puree that combines fruits, vegetables and whole grains, specially formulated for infants from 6 months old. The puree is rich in vitamins, minerals and dietary fiber, helping to establish healthy eating habits.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend of fruits, vegetables and whole grains provides a broad spectrum of nutrients in a single serving.
The product undergoes strict quality control and meets EU and FDA infant‑food standards.
All ingredients are free from added sugar, salt and artificial flavors.
Grains are pre‑processed to be easily digestible for tiny stomachs.
Packaging is made from recyclable, food‑safe material.

items.title: Rich in vitamins A and C
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision and immunity, while vitamin C aids iron absorption and protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from the grains helps normalize bowel movements and promotes a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are essential for growth, brain development, and immune function in children.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: No added salt makes the product safe for developing kidneys and the cardiovascular system.

items.title: Supports taste development
items.content: A variety of flavors helps infants become accustomed to new foods and develop balanced eating preferences.

items.title: Allergy to individual ingredients
items.content: Some children may have sensitivities to specific fruits or grains; introduce the product gradually.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Although the puree is smooth, tiny grain particles may remain; supervise the child to ensure they do not swallow large pieces.

items.title: Shelf‑life after opening
items.content: Once opened, store the product in the refrigerator and use within 48 hours.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the puree on its own or mix it with breast milk, formula, or yogurt. If needed, thin with a small amount of water to achieve the desired consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, refrigerate and consume within 2 days. Discard if the package is damaged or the puree develops an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Ice cream cone is a classic dessert consisting of a crisp waffle cone filled with a scoop of vanilla ice cream. The vanilla flavor is achieved with natural vanilla beans or flavorings, and the cone is typically baked from wheat flour, sugar, and butter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first documented ice‑cream‑in‑a‑cone recipe appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
Vanilla is one of the most popular ice‑cream flavors worldwide, used in over 30 % of all varieties.
Traditional waffle cones are formed in special presses where the batter is quickly baked under high pressure, creating the characteristic grid pattern.
In many countries the cone is served with extra toppings such as chocolate drizzle, sprinkles, nuts, or cherries.
Ice cream cones are often associated with summer fairs and street festivals.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Vanilla ice cream typically contains dairy, which provides calcium essential for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and cream in the ice cream supply vitamin B2 (riboflavin) and vitamin B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Small amount of protein
items.content: Dairy ingredients add a modest amount of protein useful for tissue repair.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Traditional ice cream contains a considerable amount of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consuming dairy ice cream.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to milk or cream.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Ice cream cones are calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on a diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the ice cream cone immediately after scooping so the cone stays crunchy. Eat it by hand, and add toppings such as chocolate sprinkles, nuts, berries, or caramel sauce if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep ice cream in the freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Store the cone in a dry place to prevent it from absorbing moisture and becoming soft. Do not leave the ice cream at room temperature for more than 30 minutes, as it will melt.

lettuce-salad-with-egg-cheese-tomato-and.title: Lettuce Salad with Egg, Cheese, Tomato and/or Carrot

content.title: About
content.content: Lettuce salad is a mix of fresh lettuce leaves, egg, cheese, tomato and carrot, with optional additional vegetables. No dressing is used, preserving the natural flavors of the ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lettuce leaves are rich in vitamins A, K and folate.
Egg provides a complete source of protein and vitamin D.
Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Carrot is high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
The lack of dressing makes the dish low‑calorie and diet‑friendly.

items.title: Vision support
items.content: Vitamin A from lettuce and beta‑carotene from carrot help maintain healthy eyesight.

items.title: Bone strength
items.content: Calcium from cheese and vitamin K from lettuce contribute to bone density.

items.title: Complete protein balance
items.content: Egg supplies all essential amino acids, important for tissue repair.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and vitamin E from cheese protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune system support
items.content: B‑vitamins from egg and folate from lettuce aid normal immune function.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs or cheese may experience reactions, up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium in certain cheeses
items.content: If salty cheese is used, monitor sodium intake, especially for hypertension.

items.title: Risk of foodborne infection
items.content: Raw eggs can harbor Salmonella; use pasteurized eggs or fully cooked eggs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad cold, tossing all ingredients together just before serving. Fresh herbs such as dill or parsley can be added for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Store eggs and cheese separately if not yet mixed with the vegetables.

content.title: About
content.content: Onion dip is a creamy snack made from cream cheese, sour cream, and flavorful onion seasonings. It has a smooth, buttery taste with a pronounced onion note and is perfect for serving with chips, vegetables, or bread.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Onion dip is a staple at American bars and picnics.
There are several variations: classic, bacon‑infused, and green‑onion versions.
The onion flavor intensifies after a few hours of refrigeration.
The original recipe uses dry onion powder, but many manufacturers add fresh onion for a brighter taste.
Onion dip is often included in party snack packs.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The cream cheese component provides calcium, which supports bone and teeth health.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: Sour cream may contain live cultures that promote gut health.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Unlike many sauces, onion dip typically contains no added sugars.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cream cheese and sour cream supply modest amounts of vitamins B2 and B12, aiding energy metabolism.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: The fats are mainly saturated, but in reasonable portions they can fit into a balanced diet.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cream cheese and sour cream contain lactose, which can cause discomfort for those who are intolerant.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The creamy texture makes the dip calorie‑rich; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy should avoid consumption.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared dip often contains added salt; individuals monitoring sodium intake should be aware.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve onion dip chilled with tortilla chips, vegetable sticks, crackers, or sliced baguette. It also works well as a sauce for burgers, sandwiches, and casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dip in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1 °C–4 °C. Once opened, it is usually good for 5–7 days. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Trifle is a layered dessert made of biscuit crumbs, custard, fruit puree or berries, whipped cream, and often topped with chocolate glaze. It is popular in the United Kingdom and the United States, where it is served in individual glasses or bowls.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Trifle originated in the 19th century as a way to use up leftover biscuits and custard.
Traditional English trifle often includes layers of berry jelly and marzipan.
In the US, chocolate mousse and nut crumble versions are common.
Trifle is frequently served at holidays such as Christmas and Thanksgiving.
Vegan versions replace cream with coconut cream and gelatin with agar‑agar.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The custard and yogurt used in trifle provide animal or plant protein that supports tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs in the custard are rich in vitamins B2 and B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from berries
items.content: Fresh berries and fruit puree supply vitamin C and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Calcium from dairy
items.content: Cream and cream cheese in trifle contribute calcium for bone health.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain biscuit crumbs add fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Trifle often contains cream, cream cheese, and eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet syrups, jelly, and fruit purees make the dessert calorie‑dense; people with diabetes should limit portions.

items.title: Raw egg content
items.content: Traditional custard is made with raw eggs; improper preparation can pose a salmonella risk.

items.title: Gluten in biscuit crumbs
items.content: Biscuit crumbs usually contain wheat; gluten‑free alternatives are needed for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve trifle chilled in clear glasses to showcase the layers. Eat with a spoon, enjoying each component. For a lighter taste, add fresh berries or a sprig of mint.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared trifle in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Add the biscuit crumb layer just before serving to retain crunch.
